claim.why_it_matters: Four-component subclauses of a statement are transcribed at heading level 3 throughout 14.9 (### 14.9.3.1 .. ### 14.9.3.4 for ALLOCATE on page 616, ### 14.9.5.1 .. ### 14.9.5.4, ### 14.9.6.x, ### 14.9.8.x, and 14.9.2.1/14.9.2.2 on page 613 itself). Emitting 14.9.2.3 and 14.9.2.4 at level 2 makes them siblings of '## 14.9.2 ADD statement' instead of children of it, so the ADD statement's syntax rules and general rules detach from the ADD statement in any outline, TOC or anchor-walk built from the markdown.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds; no content is missing or altered.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The claim is filed as kind=missing-heading, but both headings are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md at lines 25528 and 25549, with the correct numbers, the correct titles ('Syntax rules', 'General rules'), the correct order, and correct anchors <a id="section-14-9-2-3"> / <a id="section-14-9-2-4">. I compared the 300dpi render of PDF page 614 (printed folio 584) line by line against the markdown: syntax rule 1) with sub-items a) b) c), rules 2) through 6), and general rules 1) (including the displayed expressions '(operand-11 + operand-12 + ... + operand-1n)' and '(initial-evaluation + identifier-2)') and 2) are all transcribed completely and accurately. The only difference in the entire page is the '#' count on two heading lines. That is a markdown formatting attribute, which the brief names as an explicit rejection ground.

(2) THE PDF PROVIDES NO BASIS FOR ANY HEADING LEVEL. I rendered page 613 to check the premise. In the PDF, '14.9.2  ADD statement', '14.9.2.1  General', '14.9.2.2  General formats' (p.613) and '14.9.2.3  Syntax rules', '14.9.2.4  General rules' (p.614) are ALL set in the same bold face at the same point size. There is no typographic size or weight distinction between the three-component clause heading and the four-component subclause headings. The markdown's '## 14.9.2' vs '### 14.9.2.1' split is therefore a transcriber's inference from the dotted numbering depth, not something the PDF asserts. A discrepancy report needs the PDF to say something different from the markdown; here the PDF says nothing about level at all, so there is no PDF-vs-markdown conflict to ledger. The claim's own wording concedes this ('both printed in the same bold subclause style as 14.9.2.1'), which is exactly why it cannot support the conclusion.

(3) THE STATED CONSEQUENCE IS ALREADY FALSE INDEPENDENT OF THE LEVEL. The transcription inserts page furniture at every page break: '## Page 614' followed by the running header transcribed as a LEVEL-1 heading, '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)'. That H1 appears 941 times in the file (alongside 1233 '## Page N' markers). It sits directly between '## 14.9.2 ADD statement' (page 613) and '14.9.2.3 Syntax rules' (page 614). In markdown outline semantics an H1 resets the tree, so even if 14.9.2.3 were emitted as '### 14.9.2.3' it would nest under the page-614 running-header H1, NOT under '## 14.9.2 ADD statement' on page 613. Any outline, TOC, or anchor-walk built from this markdown is already partitioned by page, by construction. Changing '##' to '###' would not reattach the ADD statement's rules to the ADD statement, so the claimed harm does not follow from the claimed cause.

CONTEXT ON SCOPE. The level-2/level-3 mix is a pervasive transcription style inconsistency, not a page-614 event: across the whole file 162 four-component headings are at '##' and 620 are at '###', and within 14.9 alone the same pattern hits 14.9.1.3, 14.9.1.4, 14.9.4.3, 14.9.10.4, 14.9.11.4, 14.9.12.4, 14.9.13.3, 14.9.13.4, 14.9.14.3 and 14.9.14.4. Filing page 614 as a structural discrepancy singles out two instances of a global cosmetic artifact. If the project later wants uniform heading depth it is a whole-file normalization pass (and would have to address the running-header H1 furniture first to have any outline effect), not a spec-reconciliation finding against page 614.

No semantics, no syntax, no general rule, no section number and no citable text differs between the PDF and the markdown on this page.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a discrepancy. Both headings are present, complete and correctly numbered/titled; the entire page-614 body text matches the PDF. The only difference is that '14.9.2.3 Syntax rules' and '14.9.2.4 General rules' are emitted as markdown level-2 rather than level-3 headings. The PDF sets 14.9.2, 14.9.2.1, 14.9.2.2, 14.9.2.3 and 14.9.2.4 in one identical bold style, so it supplies no heading-level information to conflict with. The claimed outline damage is also already caused, and not cured by the level, because the transcription emits a level-1 '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' running header at the top of every page (941 occurrences), which resets the outline between page 613 and page 614 regardless. The underlying level-2/level-3 mix is a file-wide style artifact (162 four-component headings at '##' vs 620 at '###') best handled, if at all, as a global normalization pass, not as a page-614 finding.
